results.summary: This project implements a simple 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit inputs on ui[0:7] and produces a 5-bit sum on uo[0:4]. It is a Wokwi exercise intended for educational purposes, likely as part of a Tiny Tapeout workshop. The design is purely combinational, with no clock or reset. Testing involves applying all pairs of 4-bit numbers and verifying the output sum. No external hardware is required.

This design is an 8-channel LED pattern sequencer that drives up to eight LEDs with various animation patterns. It supports enable, direction control, eight pattern modes, and four speed settings via clock dividers, all controlled by the input pins. The output is an 8-bit pattern that can directly drive LEDs or be used as logic signals. Testing is done by configuring the inputs and observing the LED patterns; external LEDs are required to visualize the output. The project appears to be a workshop exercise, but the documentation contains some inaccuracies in pin descriptions.

This design is a 16-bit counter that also includes a pseudo-random number generator, according to the brief description. It takes inputs that select a multiplexer source and change the random seed, and produces a 4-bit counter output and a 6-bit random seed output. Testing requires a clock input and manipulation of the input pins to observe the outputs. The documentation is minimal and somewhat unclear, but the core functionality involves counting and random number generation.

This project is a controller for an Adafruit Charlieplex LED array, supporting up to 56 LEDs (7x8). It includes an SPI slave interface for loading custom display data, with each byte representing the brightness of one LED. On reset, it displays a brightness gradient across the array. Testing involves connecting the eight signal pins to the LED array and optionally using SPI to update the display. The design is notable for its efficient use of a single 8-pin bidirectional port to drive a large LED matrix and its SPI programmability.

This project implements AES forward S-Box circuits using direct computation rather than lookup tables, and also includes the PRESENT cipher S-Box. It provides a memory-mapped interface with 6 address pins, a read/write mode pin, an I/O latch, and an 8-bit bidirectional data bus for accessing the S-Boxes. The design is used by following specific I/O sequences detailed in the test script. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable for avoiding lookup tables in the AES S-Box implementation.
